results.question: My app has one route for /users/me and another for /users/{user_id}, and requests to /users/me keep landing in the second one. What's going wrong?
results.answer_text: The issue is that the path operation for `/users/me` must be declared before the one for `/users/{user_id}` because path operations are evaluated in order. If `/users/{user_id}` is declared first, requests to `/users/me` will be matched by it, treating `"me"` as a `user_id` parameter. To fix this, ensure the `/users/me` route is defined before `/users/{user_id}` in your code [1][2].

results.question: How do I make a route parameter swallow an entire file path with slashes in it, like home/johndoe/myfile.txt?
results.answer_text:
To make a route parameter swallow an entire file path with slashes in it, like `home/johndoe/myfile.txt`, you can declare the path parameter using the `:path` convertor in the route, like this:

```
/files/{file_path:path}
```

Here, `file_path` is the parameter name, and `:path` tells FastAPI to match any path, including slashes inside it [3].

This allows the URL `/files/home/johndoe/myfile.txt` to be matched correctly, with `file_path` containing `home/johndoe/myfile.txt` [2].

If the path starts with a leading slash, you would use a double slash in the URL, like `/files//home/johndoe/myfile.txt` [1].

results.question: How can I accept ?q=foo&q=bar and receive both values as a Python list?
results.answer_text:
You can accept multiple query parameter values like `?q=foo&q=bar` and receive them as a Python list by declaring the query parameter with a type of `list[str]` and using `Query()` in the function parameter, for example:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Query

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(q: Annotated[list[str] | None, Query()] = None):
    return {"q": q}
```

This way, FastAPI will collect all `q` query parameters into a Python list `q` inside your path operation function [1][5].

results.question: Which HTTP status codes are not allowed to carry a response body?
results.answer_text: HTTP status codes in the range `100 - 199` are for "Information" and responses with these status codes cannot have a body [1]. The status code `204` "No Content" is used when there is no content to return to the client, and so the response must not have a body [2]. Additionally, the status code `304` "Not Modified" must not have a response body [2].

results.question: My Pydantic response model has defaults on several optional fields. How do I keep those out of the JSON when the values were never actually set?
results.answer_text:
To keep default values of optional fields out of the JSON response when those values were never actually set, you can use the parameter `response_model_exclude_unset=True` in the path operation decorator. This will exclude fields with default values that were not explicitly set from the response JSON, so only the values actually set will be included [1][5].

If the data has values for fields with defaults that were explicitly set (even if they match the default), those fields will be included in the response [4]. Without this parameter, fields with default values will always appear in the response, even if not set, ensuring clients can always expect those fields to be present (possibly with default or null values) [3].

results.question: When I use a class as a dependency, how can I avoid typing the class name both as the annotation and inside Depends()?
results.answer_text:
When using a class as a dependency, you can avoid typing the class name both as the annotation and inside `Depends()` by using the shortcut provided by FastAPI. Specifically, you can declare the dependency as the type of the parameter and use `Depends()` without any parameter, like this:

```Python
commons: CommonQueryParams = Depends()
```

This way, you don't have to write the class name twice (once as the annotation and once inside `Depends()`). It is preferred to use the `Annotated` version if possible:

```Python
commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends()]
```

This shortcut works because FastAPI will "call" the class to create an instance of it when resolving the dependency [1][5].

results.question: When does the cleanup code of a dependency with yield run by default, and how can I make it finish before the response is sent?
results.answer_text: By default, the cleanup code of a dependency with `yield` runs after the response is sent to the client, as the dependency has a default `scope="request"` which means it is executed around the request and response cycle [1][2][4]. results.question: What is the difference between BackgroundTask and BackgroundTasks, and which one should I import to use as a route parameter?
results.answer_text:
The difference between `BackgroundTask` and `BackgroundTasks` is that `BackgroundTasks` can be used as a path operation function parameter in FastAPI, allowing FastAPI to handle the background tasks automatically, similar to how it handles the `Request` object. In contrast, `BackgroundTask` alone requires you to create the object manually in your code and return a Starlette `Response` including it [2].

You should import and use `BackgroundTasks` from FastAPI to use as a route parameter, as it is designed for this purpose and avoids accidentally importing the alternative `BackgroundTask` from Starlette [2][3].

results.question: Why would I choose UploadFile over declaring an uploaded file parameter as bytes?
results.answer_text: You would choose `UploadFile` over declaring an uploaded file parameter as `bytes` because `UploadFile` uses a "spooled" file, which means it stores the file in memory up to a maximum size limit and then stores it on disk after passing this limit, avoiding loading the whole file into memory. In contrast, declaring the file as `bytes` means the whole contents will be stored in memory, which works well only for small files. Additionally, when using `UploadFile`, you don't have to use `File()` in the default value of the parameter [1][3][5].

results.question: The code I put after the yield in my lifespan function never seems to run when my Docker container stops. What should I check in the Dockerfile?
results.answer_text:
You should check that you are using the **exec form** of the `CMD` instruction in your Dockerfile. Using the exec form ensures that FastAPI can shutdown gracefully and that lifespan events, including the code after `yield` in your lifespan function, are triggered properly. The exec form looks like this:

```Dockerfile
CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80"]
```

and you should avoid the shell form like this:

```Dockerfile
CMD fastapi run app/main.py --port 80
```

Make sure to always use the exec form to ensure proper shutdown behavior in FastAPI within Docker containers [2].

results.question: I mounted static files at /static. How do I link the stylesheet from a Jinja2 template, and what is the name argument on the mount for?
results.answer_text:
To link the stylesheet from a Jinja2 template when static files are mounted at `/static`, you can use the `url_for()` function inside the template to generate the URL. For example, to link a CSS file at `static/styles.css`, you would write in your template:

```jinja
<link href="{{ url_for('static', path='styles.css') }}" rel="stylesheet">
```

This will generate a link to `/static/styles.css`, which is served automatically by your FastAPI application because of the mounted static files [2][3].

The `name` argument in the mount, such as `name="static"`, gives the mounted static files application an internal name that can be used by FastAPI, for example in `url_for()`. It identifies the mounted sub-application and is used to refer to it in templates or code [1][4].

results.question: How do I let a query parameter be None?
results.answer_text:
To let a query parameter be None, you can declare it with a default value of None, making it optional. For example:

```Python
q: str | None = None
```

Alternatively, using FastAPI's `Query`, you can explicitly declare it as a query parameter with a default of None:

```Python
q: str | None = Query(default=None)
```

This makes the query parameter optional and allows it to be None [1][4].

results.question: How do I return a different status code than the default?
results.answer_text:
You can return a different status code than the default by declaring a parameter of type `Response` in your path operation function and setting the status code on it. This allows you to return a status code different from the default while still filtering and converting the data you return with a `response_model` [1]. 

Alternatively, you can return a `Response` directly, such as a `JSONResponse`, and set the additional status code directly on it [3]. 

For example, you might return `200 OK` by default but return `201 Created` when new data is created [1][3]. 

More details on changing the default status code are covered in the advanced user guide [2].

results.question: How do I return an HTML page from a FastAPI route?
results.answer_text:
You can return an HTML page from a FastAPI route by returning an `HTMLResponse` with the HTML content and status code, as shown in this example: ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse app = FastAPI() @app.get("/items/") async def read_items(): html_content = """ Some HTML in here

Look ma! HTML!

""" return HTMLResponse(content=html_content, status_code=200) ``` This returns the HTML content with a 200 status code [1]. Alternatively, you can create a function that generates and returns an `HTMLResponse` and use it in your route, specifying `response_class=HTMLResponse` to document it properly in OpenAPI: ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse app = FastAPI() def generate_html_response(): html_content = """ Some HTML in here

Look ma! HTML!

""" return HTMLResponse(content=html_content, status_code=200) @app.get("/items/", response_class=HTMLResponse) async def read_items(): return generate_html_response() ``` This approach overrides the default FastAPI behavior and properly documents the response as HTML [3][5].

results.question: How do I make every endpoint require the same dependency?
results.answer_text:
To make every endpoint require the same dependency in FastAPI, you can declare the dependency globally or include it in all path operations. FastAPI allows you to add dependencies with sub-dependencies, and it will handle calling them correctly and efficiently, including caching the results per request if needed [1][3][4]. 

Specifically, you can create a dependency function and then use it as a dependency in all your path operations, or you can use sub-dependencies to enforce common requirements like authentication or permissions across multiple endpoints [3][4]. FastAPI will ensure the dependencies are called in the correct order and only once per request unless you specify otherwise [1][2].

The provided documents do not give a direct code example of applying a dependency to every endpoint globally, but they explain how dependencies and sub-dependencies work and how to use them across multiple endpoints [1][3][4].
